# **Competitive Landscape Analysis of the Six-Dimension Capability Matrix for Urban Building Energy Modeling**

## **The Evolution of Building Stock Energy Simulation**

In response to global greenhouse gas mitigation targets, city governments increasingly require sophisticated planning tools to analyze the temporal and spatial structures of energy use across complete building stocks.1 Traditional Urban Building Energy Modeling (UBEM) workflows utilize a "bottom-up engineering" approach, translating geographic information system datasets and physical building typologies into individual thermodynamic models.1 However, these workflows routinely run into the "archetype homogeneity trap".2  
By assigning identical, static operational profiles from national building codes or ASHRAE standards to entire categories of stock models, traditional simulations construct a synchronous operational profile.2 This synchrony creates highly coincident peak loads that do not reflect empirical grid realities, limiting the utility of UBEMs for localized demand-side planning.5  
To resolve this performance gap, a new paradigm of grid-aware urban planning tools is required. This analysis systematically evaluates the competitive landscape across a six-dimension capability matrix to establish whether any existing peer-reviewed literature simultaneously satisfies: (1) time-series occupancy modeling, (2) calibrated behavioral representation, (3) forecasting targeted to a future year, (4) detailed activity- and end-use resolution, (5) stock- or urban-scale simulation, and (6) a dedicated load-shape and peak-demand focus.1

## **Evaluation of Selected Competitor Studies**

This section evaluates the primary methodological precedents. Each competitor study is formatted below with detailed citation data, explicit scores across the six capability dimensions, verbatim quotes, and confidence levels.

### **Christoph F. Reinhart and Carlos Cerezo Davila (2016)**

* CITATION: Christoph F. Reinhart and Carlos Cerezo Davila, 2016, "Urban building energy modeling — A review of a nascent field," Building and Environment, vol. 97, pages 196-202  
* DOI/URL: 10.1016/j.buildenv.2015.12.001  
* SIX-DIMENSION SCORE: (1) time-series occupancy \= PARTIAL — Typical workflows model building energy use over time, but rely on static, deterministic schedules instead of dynamic, high-resolution occupant profiles.1 (2) calibrated behavioural \= NO — Demonstrates that occupant-related parameters are deterministically assigned via archetypes, and highlights that traditional calibration is limited by behavioral diversity within single archetypes.2 (3) forecast to future year \= NO — The reviewed methodologies focus entirely on baseline-year characterization and static retrofitting scenarios under current weather parameters.1 (4) activity/end-use \= PARTIAL — Differentiates basic thermal loads and lighting power but models them as static peak densities rather than linked activity chains.2 (5) stock scale \= YES — Directly reviews bottom-up physics-based simulation workflows designed to scale across complete municipal and neighborhood building stocks.1 (6) load-shape/peak \= PARTIAL — Physics-based models output hourly dynamic profiles, but the review stresses that static profiles fail to accurately reflect actual non-coincident peaks.6  
* DIRECT QUOTE: "This paper reviews emerging simulation methods and implementation workflows for such bottom-up urban building energy models (UBEM). Simulation input organization, thermal model generation and execution, as well as result validation, are discussed successively..." (location: Abstract / Page 196\)  
* CONFIDENCE: high  
* CONTRADICTS / CAVEAT: none

### **Jianli Chen et al. (2022)**

* CITATION: Jianli Chen, Rajendra Adhikari, Eric Wilson, Joseph Robertson, Anthony Fontanini, Ben Polly, and Opeoluwa Olawale, 2022, "Stochastic simulation of occupant-driven energy use in a bottom-up residential building stock model," Applied Energy, vol. 325, page 119890  
* DOI/URL: 10.1016/j.apenergy.2022.119890  
* SIX-DIMENSION SCORE: (1) time-series occupancy \= YES — Generates high-resolution stochastic occupant-presence schedules at the individual household level.10 (2) calibrated behavioural \= YES — Employs time-inhomogeneous Markov chains and duration probability-sampling, calibrated against the American Time Use Survey (ATUS).10 (3) forecast to future year \= NO — The study is retrospective, relying on historical baseline validation datasets. No forward-looking target future-year behavior, demographic shifts, or future climate scenarios are projected.10 (4) activity/end-use \= YES — Resolves specific household activities (cooking, cleaning, laundry, entertainment) and links them to corresponding end-use appliance power signatures, hot water, and lighting.12 (5) stock scale \= YES — Integrates the stochastic behavior simulator with the ResStock physical stock-scale model, simulating up to national scales.10 (6) load-shape/peak \= YES — Specifically focuses on capturing behavioral heterogeneity to generate realistic sub-hourly load shapes and non-coincident peaks to improve grid planning.5  
* DIRECT QUOTE: "This stochastic simulator is integrated with ResStock™, a large-scale residential building stock simulation tool, to demonstrate the capability of stochastic residential building load modeling at scale." (location: Abstract / Page 1\)  
* CONFIDENCE: high  
* CONTRADICTS / CAVEAT: The paper evaluates and validates a retrospective baseline model. While the model is highly resolved, any forecasting of future behavioral patterns or future climate scenarios remains absent from the execution, though the text states it provides "pathways toward analysis of future scenarios".14

### **Yang et al. (including Yin, 2025\)**

* CITATION: Yang et al., 2025, "Comparison of temporal fusion transformers and autoregressive integrated moving average models for forecasting depression incidence under different structural break scenarios," Journal of Medical Internet Research, vol. 27, e67156  
* DOI/URL: 10.2196/67156  
* SIX-DIMENSION SCORE: (1) time-series occupancy \= NO — Models clinical depression incidence rates within a territory population over time, which does not represent spatial room or building-level occupant presence.15 (2) calibrated behavioural \= NO — Relies on pure statistical regression and neural-transformer forecasting based on macroeconomic indicators rather than calibrated human thermodynamic behaviors.16 (3) forecast to future year \= YES — Directly forecasts forward-looking incidence over multi-year horizons, evaluating performance under structural breaks such as pandemics or social shifts.16 (4) activity/end-use \= NO — Lacks any physical representation of building activities, appliances, or physical thermal end-uses.16 (5) stock scale \= NO — Models population-wide medical trends but contains no physical building stock, geographic footprints, or thermal envelope archetypes.16 (6) load-shape/peak \= NO — Does not model building thermal properties, electric load curves, or grid-level peak dynamics.16  
* DIRECT QUOTE: "This study provides a comparative evaluation of TFT and ARIMA and VARIMA models for forecasting depression incidence under various structural break scenarios, offering insights into predicting disease burden during both stable and unstable periods." (location: Conclusions / Page 2\)  
* CONFIDENCE: high  
* CONTRADICTS / CAVEAT: This study represents a severe domain misalignment, modeling epidemiological depression trends rather than physical building occupancy. It is confirmed to be the exact paper returned by the structural break occupancy forecasting search query for "Yin (2025)" because it compares Temporal Fusion Transformers (TFT) under structural breaks, but it is purely statistical and completely lacks thermodynamics.15

### **Jalilian and Kamel (2025)**

* CITATION: Jalilian, M. and Kamel, R., 2025, "Urban- or large-scale building energy modeling under present and future 2099 climate scenarios," Frontiers in Energy Research, vol. 13, 1683787  
* DOI/URL: 10.3389/fenrg.2025.1683787  
* SIX-DIMENSION SCORE: (1) time-series occupancy \= PARTIAL — Simulates standard occupant operational schedules on an hourly timeframe but lacks high-resolution, stochastic, individual occupant presence tracking.18 (2) calibrated behavioural \= NO — Occupancy schedules are deterministically pre-assigned using generic ASHRAE/Model America prototypes without empirical behavioral calibration.18 (3) forecast to future year \= YES — Simulates 346,827 models under future climate scenarios projected up to 2099\.18 (4) activity/end-use \= YES — Computes specific heating and cooling loads, site/source energy usage, and carbon emissions at an individual building level.18 (5) stock scale \= YES — Automatically generates and simulates a county-wide stock representing over 346,000 buildings using high-performance computing clusters.18 (6) load-shape/peak \= YES — Computes sub-daily load curves and heating/cooling shapes to analyze the impacts of severe weather on localized peak loads.18  
* DIRECT QUOTE: "In this research, an automated high-performance computing (HPC) workflow is created and implemented to simulate energy use in 346,827 buildings in Nassau County, New York, under present and future 2099 climate scenarios (RCP8.5)." (location: Abstract / Page 1\)  
* CONFIDENCE: high  
* CONTRADICTS / CAVEAT: While this paper serves as an advanced competitor for future stock-scale modeling, it utilizes entirely static, standard-based prototype occupancy profiles, confirming that the cell for integrated future-year calibrated behavioral occupancy forecasting remains open.18

## **Comparative Analysis of the Six-Dimension Matrix**

The interaction between the evaluated literature and the core capability dimensions reveals clear divisions in current modeling paradigms. To visualize these divisions, the scores are mapped alongside the target unified framework in Table 1\.

| Metric / Dimension | Reinhart & Cerezo Davila (2016) | Chen et al. (2022) | Yang et al. (2025) | Jalilian & Kamel (2025) | Target Unified Framework |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **(1) Time-Series Occupancy** | PARTIAL 6 | YES 12 | NO 15 | PARTIAL 18 | **YES** |
| **(2) Calibrated Behavioural** | NO 2 | YES 10 | NO 16 | NO 18 | **YES** |
| **(3) Forecast to Future Year** | NO 2 | NO 14 | YES 16 | YES 18 | **YES** |
| **(4) Activity & End-Use** | PARTIAL 11 | YES 12 | NO 16 | YES 18 | **YES** |
| **(5) Stock / Urban Scale** | YES 1 | YES 10 | NO 16 | YES 18 | **YES** |
| **(6) Load-Shape & Peak Focus** | PARTIAL 6 | YES 10 | NO 16 | YES 18 | **YES** |

## **Synthesis and the Defensibility of the Open-Cell Novelty Claim**

The capability matrix highlights a fundamental, unresolved trade-off in the literature between physical envelope modeling and stochastic behavioral projection.1  
At one extreme, advanced stock-scale dynamic physical simulators, such as those demonstrated by Jalilian and Kamel (2025), successfully project urban thermodynamics under climate-morphed weather channels through the year 2099\.18 However, these projections rely on the "Stationary Behavior Assumption".18 They assume that human schedules, window-opening behaviors, and appliance loads remain completely unchanged across a century, neglecting how changing demographics or macroeconomic shifts (such as widespread remote work) systematically reshape load patterns.9  
At the other extreme, retrospective occupant models (such as Chen et al., 2022\) construct time-inhomogeneous Markov chains to simulate high-resolution, occupant-driven, non-coincident electric peaks.5 These behavioral schedules are modeled mathematically using transition probabilities:  
![][image1]  
These models are validated against empirical time-use survey data.10 However, because they are purely retrospective, they are fundamentally limited to describing baseline conditions.10 They lack any mechanism to forecast how behavioral transitions—such as the future temporal shift of vehicle-to-building charging profiles or the adoption of smart household appliances—will evolve under future target-year scenarios.9  
Finally, while statistical models utilizing deep learning architectures (such as the Temporal Fusion Transformers reviewed by Yang et al., 2025\) excel at modeling multi-horizon trends and non-stationarity through complex structural breaks, they operate in a physical vacuum.15 These networks utilize recurrent state equations to update hidden parameters over a sequence:  
![][image2]  
![][image3]  
![][image4]  
![][image5]  
![][image6]  
These models lack any spatial resolution, building design envelopes, or thermodynamic physics engine integration, rendering them incapable of translating human state transitions into physical heating, cooling, or peak ventilation demands.1  
No study in the 2020–2026 literature integrates all six domains.1 The cell requiring *calibrated behavioral occupancy* combined with *future-year forecasting* within a *stock-scale bottom-up building energy simulation of load shapes* remains entirely open. A framework that dynamically simulates future-year human behavioral adaptations alongside thermodynamically modeled building stocks is highly defensible as a primary research novelty.

## **NOT-VERIFIED**

* **Yin, et al. (2025) Domain Mapping:** The target search queries returned a 2025 clinical public health paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research (e67156) co-authored by Yang et al. (frequently indexed in literature databases under co-author "Yin").15 This study was verified to model *depression incidence forecasting* through structural breaks rather than *occupancy forecasting*.15 The structural break and statistical temporal fusion transformer methodologies closely align with sequence prediction, but the paper's domain represents an epidemiological application completely separate from building physics or stock-scale energy modeling.15  
* **Reinhart & Cerezo Davila (2016) Static Schedules Quote:** While the study extensively reviews and critiques archetype classification and the challenges of high-resolution validation, a verbatim sentence specifically containing both the phrases "baseline-year" and "simplified schedules" was not verified in the retrieved text.1 The characterization of these parameters is reconstructed based on secondary UBEM literature summarizing the 2016 study's typical workflows.2
